cards.title: Progressive overload, and reps count as progress
cards.statement: To keep adapting, training has to get a little harder over time. Adding repetitions at the same load is real progress, not a placeholder for adding weight. Both load progression and rep progression grow muscle about equally.
cards.disputed: Nothing about the direction. How fast to progress, and by how much, varies by person.
cards.appUse: Double progression: add a rep until the top of the range, hit it twice without max effort, then take one small load step.

cards.title: Weekly volume drives growth, with diminishing returns
cards.statement: More hard sets per muscle per week produce more growth, up to a point. Past that point each extra set adds less and costs more recovery. Roughly ten or more weekly sets per muscle is where research suggests most of the benefit sits, and the exact ceiling varies by person and muscle.
cards.disputed: The exact shape at high volumes, whether there is a true plateau, and how much a set far from failure is worth. Individual response varies widely. Any specific set count is a band, not a law.
cards.appUse: Weekly effective sets per muscle compared with the user's own trailing baseline and a deliberately wide band.

cards.title: Frequency matters mostly through volume
cards.statement: How many days a week a muscle is trained matters less than how much good work it gets across the week. Splitting the same volume over more days can make each session better, but it is not required. Training a muscle a day later than ideal mainly costs session quality, not progress.
cards.disputed: Whether very high per-session volumes become low-value, which would make frequency matter more at the top end.
cards.appUse: Today's plan can swap a split without guilt. Split proposals spread focus-muscle volume over at least two days to fit more quality work, not as a rule.

cards.title: Effort can be rated by reps in reserve
cards.statement: Asking how many more reps you could have done is a valid, practical way to measure how hard a set was. In this app, easy means about four or more reps left, ideal about one to three, max about zero to one. A missing rating never counts as easy or max; it just lowers confidence.
cards.disputed: Accuracy is lower far from failure and in beginners, and people tend to underestimate how many reps they had left.
cards.appUse: The three-level effort maps to reps-in-reserve bands used by goals and by the recovery model.

cards.title: Close to failure helps growth a little; failure every set is not required
cards.statement: Sets need to be hard to be useful. Stopping a rep or two short of failure gives most of the benefit for growth and all of it for strength, at lower fatigue cost. Training to absolute failure on every set is not superior and costs more recovery.
cards.disputed: How close is close enough for growth, and whether the extra growth from the last rep is worth the extra fatigue. Researchers still disagree.
cards.appUse: Goal reps-in-reserve bands. A strength goal with max effort on every set is flagged; a growth goal is not, but recovery accounts for it.

cards.title: Heavy loads for strength; a wide rep range works for size
cards.statement: If the goal is maximal strength, lift heavy, around eighty percent of a one-rep max or more. If the goal is muscle size, loads from light to heavy work about equally as long as sets are taken close to failure.
cards.disputed: Very light loads, under roughly thirty percent, are less efficient and far more fatiguing per unit of growth.
cards.appUse: Goal rep ranges. Rep-range mismatch is a nudge for strength goals and information for growth goals.

cards.title: Recovery takes one to three days and depends on how hard and how much
cards.statement: After a hard session a muscle's ability to perform is reduced for roughly one to three days. Bigger, harder and less familiar sessions take longer; familiar sessions take less. Trained people recover faster because muscle damage shrinks with practice. Training a muscle before it has recovered mostly means a worse session, not harm.
cards.disputed: Exact hours per muscle and the size of individual variation. No table of recovery times by muscle is supported by evidence; the app's windows are priors that only widen with the user's own evidence.
cards.appUse: 24, 48 or 72 hours by effort as a prior, scaled by session volume against the muscle's own baseline, widened by the user's short-rest history, never shrunk below the effort floor.

cards.title: Planned deloads have weak evidence; easing off when signals say so is reasonable
cards.statement: Taking an easier week on a fixed schedule has not been shown to improve muscle growth, and one trial found it slightly hurt strength. What is well supported is that reduced training keeps most gains, so an easier week costs little when you actually need one.
cards.disputed: Whether deloads help people who are genuinely over-reached, which trials of healthy volunteers do not test.
cards.appUse: Never by calendar. An easier week is proposed only when several lifts decline together and effort at the same load is rising.

cards.title: Time off costs less than people fear, and regain is fast
cards.statement: A few weeks away reduces strength modestly. Muscle and strength come back faster than they were first built, because muscle keeps a memory of earlier growth.
cards.disputed: How long the memory lasts and how much of the quick regain is muscle versus skill.
cards.appUse: More than 28 days away means repeat the last load once with no increase. Copy: strength comes back fast; make the first session easy.

cards.title: Beginners: start light, add small steps often
cards.statement: New lifters respond to modest doses and progress quickly. Starting conservatively, an empty bar or the lightest dumbbell, and adding small amounts each session is safer and loses nothing. Increasing load by a few percent once you can do a rep or two beyond target is the standard guidance.
cards.disputed: There is no research table of starting weights. The specific two-clean-sessions-then-step rule is a widely taught coaching heuristic, not a trial result.
cards.appUse: Starting loads by equipment, load steps of 1, 2 or 2.5 kg capped at ten percent, and the confirm-then-step rule.

cards.title: Changing exercises: a useful reset, not a growth hack
cards.statement: Swapping a stalled exercise for a similar one can spread growth across a muscle and refresh motivation. It has not been shown to grow more muscle overall, and too much variation makes progress hard to track.
cards.disputed: Whether the observed regional growth is real or measurement. The best-supported benefit is motivation and adherence.
cards.appUse: A swap from the same movement pattern for a plateaued lift, worded as a fresh stimulus and a reset, not a fix.

cards.title: Rest longer between heavy sets
cards.statement: Two to three minutes between sets beats one minute for strength and, in trained lifters, for growth. Shorter rests are fine for lighter isolation work and for beginners.
cards.disputed: The optimum for growth on isolation exercises.
cards.appUse: Suggest two to three minutes on compound lifts for a strength goal when the rest default is short. The app does not log per-set rest, so this is advice about the default.

cards.title: Push and pull balance
cards.statement: Training the back and rear shoulders roughly as much as the chest and front shoulders is standard coaching advice for shoulder health and even development. It is reasonable, and the shoulder is where many training injuries happen, but no trial has shown that a particular ratio prevents injury.
cards.disputed: Almost everything specific. The rule is kept because lopsided programmes are common and the cost of fixing them is low.
cards.appUse: Push versus pull and upper versus lower over three weeks, with softened copy labelled as coaching consensus.

cards.title: Short sleep lowers strength performance
cards.statement: A short night measurably reduces next-day strength, especially on big compound lifts, by several percent on average. Rating effort honestly on those days keeps the coach from misreading a tired session as a real decline.
cards.disputed: Thresholds, and how much habitual short sleep matters versus one bad night.
cards.appUse: Only when Health Connect provides sleep. Suggest keeping the load and not chasing records that day. Never fires without sleep data.

cards.title: Habits form through repeated cues, slowly, and survive missed days
cards.statement: Training at a consistent time and context builds automaticity over weeks to months, about two months on average with a very wide range. Deciding in advance when and where you will train roughly doubles the odds of doing it. Missing one day does not undo the habit.
cards.disputed: Whether phone reminders help long term or just create fatigue. Evidence for reminders is modest, so they are capped hard.
cards.appUse: Learned schedule proposals and cue-timed nudges: at most one a day, none on days already trained, retired when a habit day goes cold, one tap to turn off, no streak shaming.

cards.title: One-rep-max estimates are estimates
cards.statement: Formulas that predict a one-rep max from a set of several reps correlate well with real maxes but carry bias, and they get worse as reps go up. Treat the number as about right, not exact, and never as a reason to test a true max.
cards.disputed: Which equation is best; none is exact.
cards.appUse: Epley estimate capped at ten reps, always worded as about X kg one-rep estimate.

cards.title: Acute-versus-chronic load ratios are not injury predictors
cards.statement: Comparing this week's training load with the recent average is a reasonable way to notice a sudden jump. It is not a validated predictor of injury, and the coach never presents it as one.
cards.disputed: Most of it. The ratio has known statistical pitfalls and no causal evidence.
cards.appUse: A per-muscle acute-to-chronic volume ratio is one soft input to volume-spike and deload signals. Copy never mentions injury risk.

cards.title: Tape-measure body fat is an estimate
cards.statement: The circumference method estimates body fat within a few percentage points for most people. It is useful for tracking direction over time, not for a precise number.
cards.disputed: Accuracy at the extremes of body composition and in populations unlike the original sample.
cards.appUse: Shown with about and a plus-or-minus range, and called an estimate.
